title: Elder in the garden
subtitle: A fast-growing native shrub that produces flowers and berries for food and a habitat for wildlife.
excerpt: Elder grows fast, tolerates almost any position, and produces edible flowers in June and berries in August. It fixes nothing and adds no nutrients, but it earns its place through yield, wildlife value, and the ability to coppice hard and regrow quickly.
sourceNotes: Species information from Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin, Warburg, 1952). Wildlife value from RSPB plant guide. Edibility and cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org).

glossaryTerms.definition: Cutting a woody shrub or tree to near ground level to stimulate vigorous regrowth from the base. Coppiced plants produce multiple straight stems rather than a single trunk. Elder, hazel, and willow are all traditional coppice shrubs. Coppicing keeps them productive and at a manageable size indefinitely.

content.text: Elder (Sambucus nigra) is a native UK shrub that establishes fast and tolerates almost any soil and position. In a forest garden, it earns its place through flowers in June and berries in August and September. Both are widely used in cooking and drinks.

Plant bare-root whips from November to March, or pot-grown plants in spring. Space at 2 to 3 m if growing as a shrub; closer (1 to 1.5 m) if establishing a hedge. Elder is not fussy about soil or position, but grows fastest in fertile, moist ground. It tolerates shade and coastal exposure.
Elder becomes untidy and tall if left unmanaged.

it hard in late winter every two to three years: cut to 30 to 60 cm above ground level. It regrows fast, producing soft straight stems that are easy to work with. A coppiced elder stays productive and compact.
Elder spreads by suckers and self-seeds freely. Remove suckers close to the parent plant to prevent it expanding beyond its allotted space. In a semi-wild area, allow it to spread naturally.

Pick flower heads in June when fully open and fragrant. Use fresh for cordial or fritters, or dry on a clean sheet and store for tea. Pick berries in August and September when fully black and soft. Raw elderberries cause nausea in some people: cook them before eating. Elderflowers are safe to eat raw.
